questions.question_text: A quantity obeys $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, with $Q(0)=250$ and $Q(5)=1000$. Find the exact value of $k$.

options.why: Formed the ratio the wrong way round, dividing the initial value by the later value.
Multiplied by the time instead of dividing by it when solving $5k=\ln 4$.

questions.question_text: A radioactive substance satisfies $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-0.04A$, with $t$ in years. Find its half-life, correct to the nearest year.

options.why: Used $\dfrac{1}{0.04}$ and left out the factor $\ln 2$.
Used $\log_{10}2$ instead of $\ln 2$ when solving the exponential equation.
Used $\ln 4$, which gives the time to fall to a quarter rather than to a half.

questions.question_text: A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.12P$, with $t$ in years. How long does the population take to triple, correct to one decimal place?

options.why: Used $\ln 2$, which gives the doubling time rather than the tripling time.
Divided $3$ by $0.12$ without taking the logarithm first.
Used $\log_{10}3$ instead of $\ln 3$.

questions.question_text: A sample of $800$ g decays to $700$ g in $4$ years, and satisfies $\dfrac{dm}{dt}=km$. Find the mass after $10$ years, correct to the nearest gram.

questions.question_text: A rabbit population is modelled by $P=1200e^{0.35t}$, with $t$ in years, fitted from counts taken during the first two years. Which statement best describes the limitation of this model?

options.text: It has no upper bound, so it eventually predicts more rabbits than the habitat could possibly feed.
It predicts that the population falls towards zero in the long term, which cannot happen here.
options.why: Reads $k=0.35>0$ as decay; a positive $k$ gives growth, not decline.

options.text: Its rate of increase is constant, so it cannot describe a population whose growth speeds up.
options.why: Confuses exponential growth with linear growth; $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.35P$ increases as $P$ increases.

options.text: It only gives a population for whole-number values of $t$, so it cannot be used between counts.
options.why: Treats a continuous model as a discrete one; $P=1200e^{0.35t}$ is defined for every real $t$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.35P$, so the rate of increase grows without limit as $P$ grows.
The model takes no account of the food and space the habitat can supply.
It is reliable only near the two years of data from which it was fitted.

questions.question_text: A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, with $t$ in years. It takes $9$ years for $Q$ to fall to one third of its value. Find how long it takes to fall to $5\%$ of its original value, correct to the nearest year.

options.why: Rounded $5\%$ to $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{3}\approx 3.7\%$ and counted three complete $9$-year stages.
Treated the decay as linear, losing two thirds of the original amount every $9$ years.

questions.question_text: A population is modelled by $P=3000e^{0.06t}$, with $t$ in years. Find the population after $25$ years, correct to the nearest ten.

options.why: Grew the population by $6\%$ of the initial value each year, treating the growth as linear.
Used $3000(1.06)^{25}$, the annual compounding form, instead of $3000e^{0.06\times 25}$.
